label: Normed Spaces as Geodesic Metric Spaces
notes: Open by framing the chapter question: every norm gives a metric, and the resulting space is always geodesic, yet the geometry it carries depends sharply on the shape of one object, the unit ball. We will see that strict convexity is the exact dividing line between unique and wildly non-unique geodesics.

label: From a Norm to a Metric
notes: Recall the norm axioms and define the induced distance as the norm of the difference. Stress that translation invariance and homogeneity are inherited directly, so the entire local picture is captured once by the unit ball. The triangle inequality for the metric is just the triangle inequality for the norm.

label: Straight Segments Are Always Geodesics
notes: Prove the easy half: the affine segment parametrised by arc length has length equal to the distance between its endpoints, because homogeneity makes each subsegment additive. So in any normed space a straight line realises the distance and is a geodesic. Uniqueness is the part that fails.

label: The Unit Ball Encodes the Geometry
notes: Make the unit ball the central character. Its boundary, the unit sphere, records exactly which directions cost what. Convexity of the ball is equivalent to the triangle inequality; flat faces on the boundary are equality cases. Three classic balls organise the rest of the lecture: diamond, circle, square.

label: Strict Convexity
notes: Define strict convexity precisely: the open segment between two distinct boundary points stays strictly inside the ball, equivalently equality in the triangle inequality forces the vectors to be non-negative multiples of one another. This is the property that pins down geodesics, so spend time making the boundary picture vivid.

label: Uniqueness Theorem
notes: State the central theorem: geodesics between any two points are unique if and only if the norm is strictly convex. Sketch both directions. Strict convexity forces equality in the triangle inequality only on the straight segment; a flat face produces a continuum of alternative distance-realising paths.

label: The l-p Family of Norms
notes: Introduce the p-norms on the plane and compute the three landmark balls. For p strictly between one and infinity the ball is strictly convex, so geodesics are unique. The extreme cases p equal one and p infinite have polygonal balls with flat faces, and there uniqueness collapses.

label: Non-Unique Geodesics in the l-infinity Plane
notes: Walk through the staircase construction. In the sup norm the distance between two points is the larger coordinate gap, and any monotone path staying inside the bounding rectangle has exactly that length. Draw several staircases to show a whole family of geodesics sharing the same endpoints and length.

label: The l-1 Mirror Image
notes: Show the l-one case is the same phenomenon rotated forty-five degrees. The diamond ball has flat faces too, so taxicab distance is realised by every monotone lattice-style path. Emphasise that l-one and l-infinity are linearly isometric in the plane, which is why their pathologies match.

label: Euclidean Contrast
notes: Return to the circle. The Euclidean ball is strictly convex, equality in the triangle inequality forces collinearity, and the straight segment is the only geodesic. This is the calm case that the curvature theory will demand, and it sets up why an inner product is special among norms.

label: Why CAT(0) Forces an Inner Product
notes: Connect to the larger arc of the book. The CAT(0) comparison axiom is rigid: a normed space is CAT(0) precisely when its norm comes from an inner product. Flat-faced balls fail the comparison badly, so non-positive curvature singles out Hilbert geometry among all norms.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: Summarise the dividing line: norm gives metric, segments are always geodesics, strict convexity is equivalent to uniqueness, and only inner-product norms are CAT(0). Preview that the next chapters build curvature comparison on exactly the strict, Euclidean side of this dichotomy.
